video_title: Cambria Global EW 3 ETF and 351 ETF Conversions (GEX) | Meb Faber
gist: Meb Faber hosts a Cambria webinar/Q&A pitching the November launch of GEX, a 25-basis-point global non-market-cap-weighted equity ETF being seeded via a Section 351 tax-deferred exchange, while arguing that a US CAPE ratio near 42 and an all-time-low 1.04% S&P dividend yield make concentrated, market-cap-weighted US exposure a yellow-light setup. He walks through the mechanical rules and custodian frictions of 351 conversions, defends shareholder yield over dividend and dividend-growth strategies, and lays out Cambria's 20-fund lineup plus his view that rates could and should go higher.

themes.theme: CAPE 42 and the Valuation Yellow Light

insights.claim: Meb Faber says the US Shiller CAPE ratio sits around 42 and is roughly one week of rallies from eclipsing the 1999 all-time high of about 44, which he characterizes as bubble territory rather than a mere expensive market.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A CAPE near the dot-com peak argues for trimming US market-cap beta and funding the trim with cheaper foreign, value, and small-cap exposure.
insights.quote: Remember the US is 42 today

insights.claim: Faber states that no country in his dataset has ever closed a year at a CAPE ratio of 40 and gone on to deliver above-average subsequent 10-year real returns — a batting average of zero.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Frames current US valuations as a hard constraint on the next decade's real returns, supporting lower forward return assumptions in financial plans and higher allocations to non-US assets.
insights.quote: never once in history have we found a market that closed a year, a country, at a CAPE ratio of 40 and had above average 10-year real returns

insights.claim: Faber is explicit that high valuation is a weight rather than a ceiling, noting the CAPE could easily run to 50 or 60 as Japan's did, so the expensive-and-rising setup is a 'yellow light,' not a sell signal.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Argues against outright de-risking; the actionable move is diversification and hedging rather than exiting equities on valuation alone.
insights.quote: if we know anything about markets, there's no ceiling on valuation

insights.claim: Foreign stocks and value have now outperformed for two straight years — up roughly 30% last year and another 25% this year per Faber — yet he says almost no client cares while the S&P still delivers about 15%.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A two-year relative-strength move in diversifiers that is still being ignored suggests flows into ex-US and value have room to run once US returns flatten.
insights.quote: they're definitely creaming the S&P, but no one really cares if the S&P is still doing 15%

insights.claim: Faber's four-year presidential cycle work points to the best six-to-twelve-month window beginning around October, with January historically the single biggest return month of the cycle for small cap and small cap value.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Gives a seasonal calendar overlay for adding small cap value exposure into the fourth quarter ahead of a historically strong January.

insights.claim: Faber argues market-cap weighting is structurally a buy-high-sell-low mechanism that concentrates capital in whatever has already risen most and is therefore most expensive, citing Rob Arnott's framing.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: The core intellectual case for the non-market-cap-weighted GEX product and for equal-weight or fundamentally weighted alternatives to ACWI and SPY.
insights.quote: he talks about market cap weighting and he says the problem, you know, is is they buy high and sell low, and we definitely are feeling that today

insights.claim: The two binding rules of a 351 ETF exchange are that no single contributed position may exceed 25% and the top five positions may not exceed 50%, which in practice requires roughly 11 or 12 distinct stocks or ETFs.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Anyone with a single dominant concentrated position must pair it with other holdings before contributing — a practical screen advisors can run in their head.
insights.quote: First stock can't be over 25, top five over 50.

insights.claim: ETFs contributed into a 351 exchange are looked through to their underlying holdings, so a broad fund like SPY can be paired with a concentrated single stock to satisfy the diversification tests.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: The pass-through treatment is the key workaround that makes 351 conversions feasible for holders of one dominant stock.
insights.quote: So, SPY looks through the underlying holdings.

insights.claim: Only liquid publicly listed stocks and ETFs qualify for Cambria's 351 contributions — microcap junior miners, foreign stocks into a US fund, hedge or mutual fund interests, derivatives, options, futures, leveraged ETFs, covered-call ETFs and Dogecoin are all rejected.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Sets the eligibility boundary advisors must pre-screen against before pitching a client on a conversion.

insights.claim: Faber insists a 351 conversion is tax deferral rather than a tax dodge — the cost basis carries over, so the eventual liability will likely be larger as the fund compounds, a point he says the media consistently gets wrong.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Reframes the product for compliance and client conversations, and undercuts the headline risk that a regulatory crackdown would kill the structure.
insights.quote: No, to be clear, most likely these funds will grow, they will compound, and the tax liability will actually be bigger. It's just delayed

insights.claim: Faber says the Treasury has recently been looking into 351s and long-short structures, and he actively welcomes the scrutiny because rule clarification would open the structure at wirehouses like Merrill and Morgan and flush out bad actors.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Regulatory clarity is the gating catalyst for 351 conversions scaling from niche to mainstream distribution — a headline risk that Faber reads as an upside catalyst.
insights.quote: I hope to God they take a look at 351s and clarify the rules because I think that clears the deck on making them available everywhere, Merrill and Morgan and on and on.

insights.claim: Faber calls out firms that launch a 351 portfolio and turn it over on day one as bad actors, arguing the contributed strategy should be one you'd want to own regardless of the tax benefit.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Day-one turnover is a diligence red flag investors can screen for when comparing competing 351 sponsors.
insights.quote: you'll see some um firms launch a portfolio and turn it over on on day one, which makes it look as if like the only reason they were doing this was tax related

insights.claim: Custodian support is the main structural bottleneck: Schwab has a dedicated 351 department, Fidelity refuses to do them at all, and wirehouse clients generally cannot participate unless assets are held away.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Custodian choice is now a competitive variable for RIAs; Faber reports billion-dollar RIAs moving off Fidelity partly over this and a $100 ETF fee.
insights.quote: Schwab loves it. They whole 351 department. Fidelity won't do it.

insights.claim: Faber predicts Fidelity will eventually offer 351 conversions and long-short direct indexing on its own platform while blocking outside providers, mirroring its pattern with other products.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Implies a closing window for independent ETF sponsors to capture 351 assets before the largest custodians vertically integrate the product.
insights.quote: My guess is uh they'll try to offer it on their own and ditto with a long-short direct indexing.

insights.claim: Practical minimums differ by channel: Cambria asks independent RIAs for roughly $5 million per advisor relationship across all clients, while a Schwab account can theoretically participate with as little as $150,000.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Sets the realistic entry point and shows the product is not strictly ultra-high-net-worth, even though family offices are the dominant adopter.

insights.claim: Faber estimates roughly $20 billion of 351 ETF exchanges have been done to date — hundreds of billions counting mutual fund and hedge fund conversions — and sees hundreds of billions more up for grabs over the next couple of years.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Quantifies the addressable market for the conversion trade and flags it as a client-acquisition wedge for independent RIAs before the plumbing is fully built.
insights.quote: I think there's hundreds and hundreds of billions up for grabs in the next um next couple years

insights.claim: Faber argues the single largest untapped 351 opportunity is held-away concentrated stock that advisors currently cannot bill on, citing a client with $75 million in Home Depot stock sitting outside the advisory relationship.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A concrete business-development playbook: converting held-away concentrated positions brings trillions of dollars of assets under the fee umbrella.

insights.claim: Faber says almost no founders, local VCs, private equity professionals or public-company C-suites are aware 351 conversions exist, and advises advisors to cold-call the ten public companies in their state to pitch concentrated-stock solutions.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Awareness, not demand, is the binding constraint — early distribution effort should compound disproportionately.

insights.claim: Cambria is launching its global equal-weight ETF under the ticker GEX in mid-November via a 351 seeding, with contributions needing to be arranged within about the next month and major work done by late September or early October.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A hard, dated window for anyone wanting to convert concentrated stock into diversified global equity without triggering gains this year.

insights.claim: GEX will charge a 25 basis point management fee as its only fee — below ACWI — and will hold roughly the top 500 market-cap companies across the roughly 45 to 50 investable developed and emerging countries, excluding frontier markets.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Positions GEX as one of the cheapest non-market-cap-weighted global equity ETFs available; Faber explicitly distinguishes it from EFA, which is ex-US only.
insights.quote: 25 basis points, you know, very few global equity ETFs are that low, particularly the ones that are not market cap weighted. That's less than ACWI

insights.claim: Faber thinks low-cost global non-market-cap-weighted equity could become a $50 billion category and would not be surprised if the 351-seeded funds became Cambria's largest within two years.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Sizes the sponsor's own ambition and signals where a $4.45 billion boutique expects its growth to come from.
insights.quote: If you told me in 2 years that these are our largest funds, uh I wouldn't be I wouldn't necessarily be surprised.

insights.claim: Cambria is open to running custom 351 conversions outside its two-per-year spring and fall cadence for advisors or asset managers bringing roughly $500 million, including bespoke global shareholder yield or asset allocation mandates.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Reveals a negotiable, capacity-driven product pipeline — large allocators can effectively commission their own tax-deferred vehicle.

themes.theme: Shareholder Yield vs the Dividend Complex

insights.claim: Faber argues that for a taxable investor focused on compounding, dividends are actively harmful because they force a taxable distribution that must then be reinvested — the logic behind Cambria's TAX fund targeting low-to-no dividend yield stocks.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Implies high-dividend funds carry a persistent after-tax drag; Faber thinks the tax-managed low-dividend concept is eventually a $100 billion category with no competitors.
insights.quote: if you're a taxable investor whose focus is compounding, the last thing in the world you want is dividends

insights.claim: The S&P 500 currently yields an all-time-low 1.04% dividend yield, which Faber says makes the tax advantage of low-dividend strategies matter far less versus the index than versus dedicated high-dividend funds.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Locates where the after-tax edge actually lives: against 3-4% yielding dividend products, not against the cap-weighted index.
insights.quote: the S&P yields an all-time low dividend yield of 1.04%

insights.claim: Faber says the average US stock is a net share issuer, so gross buyback announcements are misleading — a company announcing a 5% buyback while granting 7% in stock-based compensation has a negative net buyback yield.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Screening on net shareholder yield rather than gross buybacks or dividend yield is presented as the operative edge; dilution is the hidden negative carry in most dividend strategies.
insights.quote: Average stock in the US is a issuer. It means you're getting diluted.

insights.claim: Cambria's three original shareholder yield ETFs — SYLD, FYLD and EYLD — have all now reached 10-year track records and rank top decile, in some cases top 5%, versus their categories.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Provides the live out-of-sample evidence Faber uses to argue buyback-inclusive yield beats dividend-only screens.

insights.claim: Faber contends the dividend-growth chart every asset manager publishes rests on a faulty study, and that when properly screened dividend growth delivers roughly market-like returns while dividend yield is the better strategy.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Directly challenges the marketing basis of a large ETF category; if correct, dividend-growth funds are paying a narrative premium for market returns.

insights.claim: Faber explains large asset managers have not launched shareholder yield funds because they are trapped in 'narrative jail' after 30 years of promoting dividend growth, meaning adoption requires an entirely new product rather than a strategy change.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Explains why a demonstrably better strategy stays uncrowded — an incumbent-inertia moat that benefits boutique sponsors like Cambria.
insights.quote: they're in sort of a narrative jail where if they've been promoting dividend growth for 30 years, all of a sudden they say, just kidding, let's incorporate buybacks

insights.claim: Faber names three universal allocation mistakes — US-only exposure, market-cap weighting with no value or small/mid tilt, and zero real assets (commodities, commodity equities, TIPS, global REITs) — and adds the absence of trend following as his fourth.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A four-point audit an allocator can run against any retail, professional, or institutional portfolio right now.

insights.claim: Faber allocates most of his own money to TRTY, Cambria's largest allocation ETF, which combines roughly half buy-and-hold global allocation (GAA-style) with half trend following (GMOM-style) that can go 100% cash and bonds.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Skin-in-the-game signal for the buy-and-hold plus trend barbell as the manager's preferred all-weather structure.
insights.quote: which is called Trinity, TRTY, uh which I think is our largest allocation ETF, and it's what I do with most of my money

insights.claim: Cambria's recently launched endowment-style allocation ETF runs 140% gross leverage targeting Yale-endowment-like returns, with roughly 70% equities, 30% fixed income, 20% real assets and 20% alternatives.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A leveraged multi-asset wrapper that Faber explicitly warns will be volatile — sizing matters more than the return target.

insights.claim: Cambria's VAMO is currently 50% hedged with futures — its hedge can range from zero to 100% — precisely because the broad market is expensive but still rising.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A live positioning readout: the manager is running half-hedged equity exposure, a concrete expression of the yellow-light valuation view.
insights.quote: Currently, it's 50% hedged cuz the broad market's expensive but going up.

insights.claim: GVAL selects roughly the cheapest third of about 45 countries — 12 to 15 markets — using CAPE plus cash flow, dividends and book value, then buys the top 10 stocks from each market's top 30 by market cap, rebalancing once a year.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A top-down country-value process that lands in high-single-digit to low-double-digit CAPE markets and produces very different holdings than bottom-up value screens.

insights.claim: Faber says Cambria closed its FAIL foreign-stock tail-risk fund because US investors barely own foreign stocks and, where they do, believe them too cheap to hedge — and they hedge foreign beta with more expensive US index puts instead.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Illustrates that product survival depends on adoption, not strategy quality, and reveals a cross-hedging behavior in how investors actually buy protection.

insights.claim: Faber says Cambria missed the trade on its BAIL long-bond tail-risk fund because rates had already moved from zero to five percent, but may still launch a corporate and junk bond tail-risk fund since razor-thin spreads will eventually blow out.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Flags compressed credit spreads as the next tail-risk hedging opportunity Cambria wants to productize.

themes.theme: Fixed Income Yield Gap and the Debt Trade

insights.claim: Faber calls insufficient yield in fixed income one of his hills to die on — relative to T-bills there is not enough spread compensation, so Cambria's value-based bond fund and its trend fund currently show little overlap.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Argues for staying in T-bills over reaching into credit sleeves until spreads widen — a positioning stance an allocator can copy directly.
insights.quote: one of my hills to die on is there's not enough yield in fixed income

insights.claim: Faber believes rates could and should go higher and says this would surprise a lot of people, positioning himself as a lone wolf on the view.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A contrarian duration call against consensus expectations for lower rates; short duration and floating exposure would benefit if right.
insights.quote: it feels like uh rates could and should go higher, which I think would surprise a lot of people

insights.claim: On the national debt, Faber concludes all roads lead to inflation and that the correct response is to be an owner of assets, noting US households are an order of magnitude more invested in equities than European households.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Frames equity and real-asset ownership as the default hedge against fiscal deterioration rather than any specific debt trade.
insights.quote: all roads to me lead to inflation

insights.claim: Faber says concentrated positions are on average a terrible idea regardless of survivorship-biased success stories, invoking Enron and CMGI against the Nvidia and Berkshire winners people cite.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: The demand-side rationale for the entire 351 conversion business; the research base on concentrated stock risk is what advisors should lead with.
insights.quote: concentrated positions on average are a horrible, terrible very bad idea

insights.claim: Faber argues commission- and load-based brokers are a dying profession that will not be future-proof in a world of AI and automation, while fee-based fiduciaries can charge normally on a converted 351 ETF like any other holding.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Cheap 25bp ETF wrappers plus tax-deferred conversions structurally favor the fee-based RIA channel over transactional brokerage.
insights.quote: that's a dying profession that I think is um is not going to be future-proof in a world of AI and automation

insights.claim: Cambria is approaching $4.45 billion in assets across 20 funds in its 20th year, with several funds up 20-25% this year as the bear-market-diversification thesis from its earlier paper plays out in reverse.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Establishes the sponsor's scale and why it can now afford to launch low-fee, innovative products — relevant to whether GEX gets the support to survive.

insights.claim: Faber places Cambria as a 'first cousin' to Dimensional and Research Affiliates, endorsing both as gold-star shops while dismissing roughly 80% of the industry's products as expensive and tax-inefficient.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Maps the factor/systematic peer set an allocator should be comparing GEX and Cambria's shareholder yield funds against.
